cues.text: Let us now turn to professional standards and the Nigerian context, which brings together the ethical codes that guide practitioners and the legal and practical environment in which Nigerian technology professionals actually work.
We begin with two major professional codes.
First, the ACM Code of Ethics.
ACM is the Association for Computing Machinery.
This code emphasises a set of commitments: the public good, avoiding harm, honesty, fairness, respect for privacy and confidentiality, competence, quality, and robust security.
Notice how these fit together.
Public good and avoiding harm tell you whose interests come first.
Honesty and fairness govern how you treat people.
Privacy and confidentiality protect the people whose information you handle.
Competence, quality and robust security describe the standard of work you owe them.
Second, the ACM/IEEE software engineering code.
IEEE is the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers.
This code emphasises public interest.
It then addresses clients and employers, whose interests must be pursued consistently with the public interest.
It goes on to product quality, independent judgment, ethical management, the profession itself, colleagues, and ongoing learning.

So there is a clear ordering of loyalties here: the public interest sits above the interests of a particular client or employer, and an engineer must keep independent judgment even when under commercial pressure.
Now, an important qualification.
Professional codes guide decisions, but they do not substitute for law or for professional accountability.
A code is not a statute, and following a code does not excuse you from legal duties.
Likewise, a code does not remove your personal responsibility for your own professional conduct.
Keep these three things distinct: ethical principles, professional codes, and enforceable law.
Next, the relevant Nigerian legal context.
It includes the NDPA 2023, which is the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, and the NDPC, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission.
It includes the historical NDPR, the Nigeria Data Protection Regulation, which you should treat as part of the history of the field rather than the current principal instrument.
It also includes the Cybercrimes Act as amended, the Copyright Act 2022, contracts, and applicable sector regulations.
The source gives a crucial instruction here: determine scope rather than assume every rule applies.
Not every law applies to every product or every organisation.
A professional must work out which rules actually reach the system in question, rather than assuming all of them do, or none of them.
Two examples show how this works.
A healthcare app must consider sensitive data, accessibility, clinical safety, and applicable professional and sector duties.
Think of the stakeholders: patients, whose health information is sensitive; clinicians, who rely on the app; and the organisation that builds it.
Accessibility matters because patients differ in ability.
Clinical safety matters because errors can harm people directly.
A financial app must consider transaction integrity, fraud, identity, consumer protection, and privacy.
Here the stakeholders are customers, whose money and identity are at stake, and the provider, which must keep transactions accurate and secure.
Transaction integrity means transactions are recorded correctly.
Fraud and identity concern who is really acting.
Consumer protection and privacy concern fair treatment and the handling of personal data.
Finally, the practical environment.
The challenges include infrastructure gaps, cost, digital literacy, informal processes, limited skills, weak enforcement, and pressure to ship quickly.
The opportunities include mobile-first and low-bandwidth design, inclusive research, local languages, community collaboration, secure open standards, training, and professional leadership.
So the same context that creates difficulty also creates room for thoughtful, well-fitted design.
But the source ends with a firm caution: do not equate local constraints with permission to lower safeguards for vulnerable users.
Limited infrastructure, tight budgets, weak enforcement or deadline pressure explain why things are hard.
They do not justify weaker protection for people who are most at risk.
Returning to the codes we began with, avoiding harm and serving the public interest remain the standard, whatever the local conditions.
